lectures.title: Ledgers with a Gatekeeper - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: An analyst who has read Ethereum transfers on day 3 opens a USDT transfer on Tron. Which skill carries over?
questions.correct_answer: Reading it as on Ethereum: an address holds a balance, and a USDT transfer is a contract call that emits a Transfer log.
incorrect_answers: Reading it as on Bitcoin: coins are spent from earlier outputs, and a USDT transfer is a new output script now.
Reading it as on a permissioned ledger: the operator keeps the records and shows a USDT transfer only to members.
None of it, since Tron has its own account and token design and a USDT transfer there needs a separate reading method.
questions.explanation: Tron is an account chain built on Ethereum's ideas. A balance per address, tokens as contracts and transfers as Transfer logs all carry over; only the address format and the fee model are new.
questions.lesson_block: Tron works like Ethereum, with T-addresses

specific_source.anchor: Tron works like Ethereum, with T-addresses

questions.question_stem: A report on a Tron case says its USDT moved only in blocks that were solidified. What does that tell a reader about those blocks?
questions.correct_answer: At least 19 distinct active Super Representatives had produced a block at or above their height, so they cannot change.
incorrect_answers: At least 19 exchanges had received funds from them, so the blocks were accepted by the services holding the USDT.
All 27 Super Representatives had each signed the block, so every elected producer confirmed the USDT transfer in that block.
Tether had approved the block before it was added, so the issuer had checked each USDT transfer in it against its list.
questions.explanation: Tron calls a block solidified once at least 19 distinct active Super Representatives have produced a block at or above its height. An analyst reads solidified data so an answer never rests on a block that could still change.

questions.question_stem: A colleague says the 27 Super Representatives that produce Tron's blocks can freeze a USDT balance. Is that right?
questions.correct_answer: No. They only make blocks; the freeze is called by the owner of the USDT contract, which is a multisignature wallet.
incorrect_answers: Yes. Any 19 of them can vote to blacklist an address, because they control which transactions the whole Tron network includes.
No. They can only vote on a freeze, and Tether's owner wallet then carries out whatever the elected producers decided.
Yes. They run the network, so each can add an address to the blacklist, and Tether's owner wallet only reviews the list.
questions.explanation: On Tron the Super Representatives make the blocks, but only the owner of the USDT contract can call addBlackList. Tether, not the network, is the gatekeeper for USDT.
questions.lesson_block: USDT on Tron: same freeze, same owner rule

specific_source.anchor: USDT on Tron: same freeze, same owner rule

questions.question_stem: An address holds USDT but no TRX, and still sends USDT onward. How can that be?
questions.correct_answer: Another account delegated Energy to it, and a USDT transfer, being a contract call, is paid for in Energy.
incorrect_answers: Tron charges no fee for token transfers, so a USDT move needs no Energy or Bandwidth from any account.
The USDT contract takes its fee out of the amount sent, so the holder never needs TRX or Energy to move USDT.
Bandwidth alone pays for contract calls, so the free daily Bandwidth quota covers a USDT transfer for any address.
questions.explanation: A USDT transfer is a contract call, so it needs Energy. Energy has no free quota: an account must stake TRX, receive delegated Energy, or burn TRX. An address with no TRX can therefore move USDT if another account delegates Energy to it.
questions.lesson_block: Energy pays for a USDT move: who staked it?

specific_source.anchor: Energy pays for a USDT move: who staked it?

questions.question_stem: Besides who sent a Tron USDT transfer, what else should the analyst note about it?
questions.correct_answer: The account that supplied the Energy, because it paid for the move and so is itself a link to the sender.
incorrect_answers: The validator that made the block, since the producer that made it was paid in USDT by the sender for the work.
The exchange that burned the TRX, since every Energy payment on Tron is made by some exchange for its users.
Nothing more, since the sender is the only party to a transfer and others' fees carry no information.
questions.explanation: Energy delegation is an on-chain relationship between two accounts. Noting who paid for a move, not only who sent it, can connect addresses that otherwise look unrelated.

questions.question_stem: Why does a US analyst on a stablecoin case need to know Tron, not Ethereum alone?
questions.correct_answer: About half of all USDT in circulation sits on Tron, so a USDT case will often run through that chain.
incorrect_answers: Tron has more validators than Ethereum, so its transfers are easier to follow than the same USDT moves there.
Tether can freeze USDT only on Tron, so any case that needs a freeze has to run through that network first.
Ethereum no longer carries USDT, so every stablecoin case that is traced today ends up on the Tron network.
questions.explanation: By the lesson's figures (as of 31 Oct 2026), 51% of USDT is on Tron and 39% on Ethereum. Stablecoins carry most illicit volume, so students will meet Tron in most USDT cases.
questions.lesson_block: Half of all USDT sits on Tron

specific_source.anchor: Half of all USDT sits on Tron

questions.question_stem: A draft assessment says USDT on Tron is 'half of supply', copied from a slide dated 31 Oct 2026. What should the analyst do before quoting it?
questions.correct_answer: Read the current figure and state the date of the read, because supply by chain changes daily.
incorrect_answers: Quote the slide figure, since a share published by a course is a settled fact that needs no date.
Round the figure to the nearest tenth, since a share of a moving total cannot be stated.
Drop the figure, since supply by chain cannot be read from public data and any share is a guess.
questions.explanation: Facts that change carry an as-of date. Supply by chain moves daily, so the analyst reads the present figure and states the date of the read.

questions.question_stem: Today's read of isBlackListed for a Tron address returns true. A draft says the address was frozen before the suspect's transfers. What is wrong?
questions.correct_answer: Today's status does not show when the freeze happened; set the AddedBlackList event's time against the transfers.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because a true result means the address has been on the blacklist since its first USDT transaction.
The wording, because a blacklisted address cannot have sent transfers and so the draft's claim is impossible.
The block height, because isBlackListed only answers for blocks that are older than 19 confirmations when they are read.
questions.explanation: isBlackListed answers for the block you read it at. The AddedBlackList event gives when the freeze was made, and that time, set against the transfers, shows whether the funds had already left.
questions.lesson_block: A freeze is true only as of the read

specific_source.anchor: A freeze is true only as of the read

questions.question_stem: An address reads as not blacklisted today. Can the analyst say it was never frozen?
questions.correct_answer: No. A later RemovedBlackList event can undo a freeze, so the event history must be read and each status dated by block.
incorrect_answers: Yes. A blacklist entry can never be removed once added, so a clear status today proves that no freeze ever happened to it.
Yes. Tether freezes only through destroyBlackFunds, and the address would then show a zero balance rather than a status.
No. A freeze is shown only by an address's balance, so the analyst must check it for a change in the amount of USDT held.
questions.explanation: Status read today may differ from status then. Tether's contract has a RemovedBlackList event that undoes a freeze, so the analyst writes the block and the date read beside every freeze answer.
questions.lesson_block: A freeze is true only as of the read

specific_source.anchor: A freeze is true only as of the read

questions.question_stem: On what does trust rest in a permissioned ledger, where it rested on costly work in Bitcoin and on stake in Ethereum?
questions.correct_answer: Identity and policy: only organizations the operator admits take part, each known by a certificate from its own authority.
incorrect_answers: Computing power: the admitted organizations compete to solve a puzzle before each of them may add a block to it.
Staked coins: each admitted organization locks a larger deposit that is lost if it signs a record the others reject.
Anonymity: the operator hides every member's name so that no organization can be pressed to alter its records.
questions.explanation: In Hyperledger Fabric a membership service provider maps each participant to a certificate from its organization's authority. The operator admits members and writes the rules.
questions.lesson_block: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes

specific_source.anchor: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes

questions.question_stem: Why is a committed transaction on a permissioned ledger final, with no waiting for confirmations?
questions.correct_answer: Known participants agree once the required quorum has signed, so no mining is needed and no reorganization follows.
incorrect_answers: The operator keeps a private copy of every block, so a block the members dispute is replaced from that copy.
The central bank or operator signs each block alone, so a block that it has signed can never be disputed later.
Every member holds a full copy of the ledger, so the one that has the longest chain at the time wins the dispute.
questions.explanation: Fabric trades mining for identity and policy. Once the required approvals are in, the transaction is committed and final.
questions.lesson_block: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes

specific_source.anchor: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes

questions.question_stem: Funds trace from Tron into a bank's permissioned ledger. What can the analyst still say?
questions.correct_answer: Everything up to the edge, and who the operator is; the records exist but sit with the operator and its members.
incorrect_answers: Everything, because the operator publishes its ledger on a public explorer once an outside transfer is first received.
Nothing at all, because a trace that reaches a permissioned ledger is void and cannot support any statement.
Where the funds went next, because the public Tron record keeps following the funds inside the bank ledger.
questions.explanation: An outsider sees no node, no explorer and no copy of the ledger. The analyst names the operator and states that the trace stops at its edge.
questions.lesson_block: The trace stops at the operator's edge

specific_source.anchor: The trace stops at the operator's edge

questions.question_stem: A Fabric channel has a private data collection. What do channel peers outside the collection hold?
questions.correct_answer: Only a hash of the private data, while a defined subset of organizations on the channel holds that data.
incorrect_answers: The full data in an encrypted form, since every peer keeps a copy that only the subset can read.
Nothing at all, since peers outside the collection do not learn that a private transaction was made.
A summary of the data, because the orderer publishes it to the whole channel when it commits the private block.
questions.explanation: A collection narrows who sees data within a channel. Other peers get only a hash, and the orderer does not see the private data.

specific_source.anchor: The trace stops at the operator's edge

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson treat a CBDC kept on a ledger like a Fabric network, when it comes to what an analyst can see?
questions.correct_answer: It is a permissioned ledger with the central bank as the operator, so the trace stops at its edge.
incorrect_answers: It is a public ledger like Bitcoin, so the central bank is only one of many nodes that anyone can query.
It is a stablecoin issued by a bank, so the central bank can freeze it by the same owner function as USDT.
It is a ledger that no one runs, so there is no operator to name and the analyst treats it as unknowable.
questions.explanation: A central bank digital currency on a ledger is run by a central bank that admits participants. The analyst can name the operator but cannot read the ledger from outside.
questions.lesson_block: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs

specific_source.anchor: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs

questions.question_stem: A case follows frozen Tron USDT and later enters a CBDC ledger. How should the analyst state who could stop the money at each point?
questions.correct_answer: On Tron, Tether, by freezing, dated by block; in the CBDC ledger, the central bank as operator, seen only up to its edge.
incorrect_answers: On Tron, the 27 Super Representatives, by vote; in the CBDC ledger, the same group, since both ledgers are run alike.
On Tron, no one, since the chain is open; in the CBDC ledger, Tether, which holds the keys for the central bank.
On Tron, Tether, as read today; in the CBDC ledger, any member, since each can read and stop the other's payments.
questions.explanation: Each ledger has a gatekeeper to name. For USDT the issuer is the gatekeeper and its freeze is dated by block; on a permissioned ledger the operator is, and the trace stops at its edge.

questions.question_stem: In the instructor's Fabric demo, peers are taken offline and new writes fail. Why?
questions.correct_answer: The endorsement policy names whose peers must sign a write, so with too few of them the write is not valid.
incorrect_answers: The ledger is mined by those peers, so with fewer of them online the puzzle for the next block cannot be solved.
The orderer needs every peer online to read each write, so a missing peer stops the write from being ordered.
The certificate authority revokes a member's certificate when its peer goes offline, so writes fail.
questions.explanation: Membership and endorsement are separate. The endorsement policy decides whose endorsement counts, and without enough signing peers the write is not valid.
